\chapter{The Turning Season}
\label{ch:sa-the-turning-season}
\hlchaptermodality{61}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a season in Sanskrit and write the independent vowel \sk{ऋ} that its name begins with.}

Complete SA-S225-letter-vocalic-r and name the word you already say that begins with \sk{ऋ}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ṛtuḥ]{\sk{ऋतुः} (ṛtuḥ) — a season}

\label{lesson:SA-C61-rtu}



\begin{quote}
What does \textbf{\sk{।}} mark? Then say \textbf{\sk{दिनम्}} and \textbf{\sk{मासः}}, and say which names the longer stretch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{ऋतुः}}
\textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}} (\emph{ṛtuḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a season\textquotedblright{}.

You have a word for a day. This is the word for the largest division of the year below the year itself — and in India the count is traditionally \textbf{six} rather than four.

The word comes from the root \textbf{\sk{ऋ}}, \textquotedblleft{}to go, to move\textquotedblright{} — a season is a \textbf{turn that comes round}. That is worth holding, because the same root gives one of the most important words in the whole language: \textbf{\sk{ऋतम्}} (\emph{ṛtam}), the fixed order of things, the way the world turns as it should. A season is one turn of that order.

The far end of that family reaches English. From the same root, through Latin \emph{rītus}, comes English \textbf{rite} — a thing done at its proper turn. And \emph{ars}, \textquotedblleft{}art\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin: skill as things fitted together in their proper order.

Look at the first letter. \textbf{\sk{ऋ}} is the independent vowel \emph{ṛ} — and it is the first word in this book that begins with it. You have written its small form, the \textbf{\sk{ृ}} hanging under a consonant, in \textbf{\sk{गृहम्}} and \textbf{\sk{हृदयम्}}. This is the full-size letter it becomes when nothing carries it.

The next lesson draws it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A season, and a word that needs a letter you have never been shown whole.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{ṛtuḥ}, said once slowly and once at speed
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṛtuḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dinam}, then \emph{māsaḥ}, and place \emph{ṛtuḥ} between them by length
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}} and at \textbf{\sk{गृहम्}}, and find the same vowel in two shapes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}} mean, and how many seasons does the Indian count traditionally have? (\textquotedblleft{}A season\textquotedblright{}, and six.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṛ]{\sk{ऋ} — the independent vowel}

\label{lesson:SA-S225-letter-vocalic-r}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}} and what it means. Then find the \textbf{\sk{ृ}} under the \textbf{\sk{ग}} in \textbf{\sk{गृहम्}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: \sk{ऋ}}
\textbf{\sk{ऋ}} — \emph{ṛ}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel}: the full-size letter this vowel wears when it opens a word and has no consonant to lean on. You have known its other half for a long time — inside a word the same vowel is the small \textbf{\sk{ृ}} written under the consonant, which you have been reading in \textbf{\sk{गृहम्}} and \textbf{\sk{हृदयम्}} for a long while.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a short upper-left shoulder turning into a diagonal hook
  \item a separate rounded middle body continuing into the lower tail
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ऋ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}} \emph{ṛtuḥ} — a season
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ऋ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the open upper-left tip, sweep right through the short shoulder, then turn down-left through the diagonal hook
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at the middle body's left edge, loop anticlockwise round its little ball, then run down to the right and swing the lower bowl left, round the bottom, and out to the right without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified four-stroke modern printed teaching form; Hindi normally reads the inherited vowel as ri
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{ऋ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ऋ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{ऋतुः}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ऋ} three times, saying \emph{ṛ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the full \textbf{\sk{ऋ}} at the front of \textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}} and the small \textbf{\sk{ृ}} under the \textbf{\sk{ग}} of \textbf{\sk{गृहम्}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ऋ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ṛ}}.) Name the word you already say that begins with it.
